claims.claim: Michael Scriven proposed the terms formative and summative in 1967 to name two roles evaluation might play with respect to a curriculum: a role in the ongoing improvement of the curriculum, and a role enabling administrators to decide whether the finished curriculum represented a sufficient advance on the available alternatives to justify adoption.

Two years later Benjamin Bloom applied the same distinction to the evaluation of student learning, describing formative evaluation as brief tests used by teachers and students as aids in the learning process, and stating that although such tests may be graded and used in the judging and classificatory function, formative evaluation is much more effectively used when it is separated from the grading process.

On Wiliam's reading of these early uses, 'formative' cannot be a property of an assessment: assessments are formative if and only if something is contingent on their outcome and the information is actually used to alter what would have happened in the absence of that information. What makes an assessment formative is not the length of the feedback loop, where it takes place, who carries it out, or who responds.

Formative assessment operates on a continuum of cycle lengths: long-cycle between instructional units (four weeks to a year or more), medium-cycle between lessons (one day to two weeks), and short-cycle within a single lesson (five seconds to one hour). A question that requires every student to respond creates what Wiliam calls a moment of contingency, at which instruction can change direction in light of evidence.

The CCSSO FAST SCASS defined formative assessment in 2006 as a process used by teachers and students during instruction that provides feedback to adjust ongoing teaching and learning to improve students' achievement of intended instructional outcomes, and revised it in 2018 to a planned, ongoing process used by all students and teachers during learning and teaching to elicit and use evidence of student learning to improve student understanding of intended disciplinary learning outcomes and support students to become self-directed learners.

The FAST SCASS states that defining formative assessment as a process was taken as a direct counter to the concept of formative assessment as an instrument or specific assessment, and that the 2018 revision names five practices that must be integrated: clarifying learning goals and success criteria within a broader progression of learning; eliciting and analyzing evidence of student thinking; engaging in self-assessment and peer feedback; providing actionable feedback; and using evidence and feedback to move learning forward by adjusting learning strategies, goals, or next instructional steps.

The FAST SCASS distinguishes formative assessment from other assessment labels: summative assessment is designed to provide information about the level of student, school or program success at an end point in time and is administered after the conclusion of instruction; interim (also called benchmark, common or quarterly) tests are administered periodically through the year to serve predictive, evaluative and/or instructional functions; and diagnostic assessments are evidence-gathering procedures indicating which targeted subskills or enabling knowledge a student possesses, used for the subset of students not making sufficient progress.

The FAST SCASS reports that many interim tests were originally marketed as though they were themselves formative assessments, quotes Heritage's statement that the core problem is the false but widespread assumption that formative assessment is a particular kind of measurement instrument rather than a process, and states that after scrutiny of research on the effectiveness of interim assessments there was at that time no meaningful evidence that such assessments enhance student learning.

The FAST SCASS states that curriculum-embedded assessments are more apt to be formative when non-graded and used by both teachers and students to support further learning, and that if they are used in the grading process the only feature distinguishing them from other summative assessment processes is the way they have been blended into ongoing instructional activities.

Manitoba Education / WNCP, in a document written by Lorna Earl and Steven Katz, sets out three distinct but inter-related purposes of classroom assessment: assessment for learning, designed to give teachers information to modify and differentiate teaching and learning activities; assessment as learning, a process of developing and supporting metacognition in which the student is the critical connector between assessment and learning; and assessment of learning, which is summative in nature and confirms what students know and can do. It notes that some authors use only two categories, and states that it is very difficult, and sometimes impossible, to serve three different assessment purposes at the same time.

Kluger and DeNisi's 1996 meta-analysis of 607 effect sizes from 23,663 observations found that feedback interventions improved performance on average (d = .41) but that over one third of the feedback interventions decreased performance; their Feedback Intervention Theory holds that feedback effectiveness decreases as attention moves up a hierarchy of control toward the self and away from the task.

Attaching a grade to written feedback tends to remove the benefit of the feedback. Butler's 1988 experiment with fifth- and sixth-grade classes compared numerical grades, individual comments, and grades plus comments; Black and Wiliam summarize the wider evidence by stating that if pupils are given only marks or grades they do not benefit from the feedback, and that feedback improves learning when it gives specific guidance on strengths and weaknesses, preferably without any overall marks.

The frequently quoted claim that formative assessment produces effects of 0.4 to 0.7 standard deviations originates in Black and Wiliam's 1998 Phi Delta Kappan article 'Inside the Black Box', which stated that typical effect sizes of the formative assessment experiments were between 0.4 and 0.7 and that these were larger than most found for educational interventions.

That range is not an established finding. Kingston and Nash reviewed more than 300 K-12 studies, found only 13 with sufficient information to calculate effect sizes, and from 42 independent effect sizes obtained a weighted mean effect size of 0.20 under a random-effects model, with estimates of 0.32 for English language arts, 0.17 for mathematics and 0.09 for science; they concluded that the commonly claimed effect of about 0.70 (or 0.40-0.70) is not supported by the existing research base.

Bennett's critical review concluded that the term formative assessment does not yet represent a well-defined set of artefacts or practices, that the breadth of current definitions permits implementations with highly variable outcomes, and that the magnitude of commonly made quantitative claims for its effectiveness is suspect, deriving from untraceable, flawed, dated or unpublished sources.

Wiliam, one of the two authors of the 1998 summary, wrote in a 2006 commentary that his own reading of the research suggested medium-cycle formative assessments had shown only modest impact on student learning, and that the studies showing impact tended to be those that changed teachers' day-to-day and minute-to-minute classroom practice.

The 2009 IES/What Works Clearinghouse practice guide on using student achievement data to support instructional decision making assigns a Low level of evidence to all five of its recommendations, including 'make data part of an ongoing cycle of instructional improvement' and 'teach students to examine their own data and set learning goals'; IES states that a Low rating indicates the panel did not identify a body of research demonstrating effects of the practice on student achievement, and should not be read as a judgment that the recommendation is unimportant.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How large is the effect of formative assessment on achievement?
positions: Black and Wiliam (1998) reported typical effect sizes between 0.4 and 0.7, larger than most educational interventions, and that gains were greatest for low achievers.
Kingston and Nash (2011) found only 13 usable studies out of more than 300 and obtained a weighted mean effect size of 0.20, concluding the 0.40-0.70 claim is unsupported.

Bennett (2011) argued that the quantitative claims trace to untraceable, flawed, dated or unpublished sources, and that 'formative assessment' is too loosely defined for a single effect size to be meaningful.
Wiliam himself (2006) wrote that medium-cycle formative assessment had shown only modest impact in his own reading of the literature.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the 0.4-0.7 range only as a historical claim from a specific 1998 article, immediately paired with the later meta-analytic and critical literature and with Wiliam's own qualification. It states no single effect size as the effect of formative assessment, and attributes the direction of the evidence (mechanism plausible, magnitude unsettled and implementation-dependent) rather than a number.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Are interim or benchmark tests formative assessments?
positions: Vendors and many districts have marketed and used interim/benchmark products under the label 'formative assessment'.

The CCSSO FAST SCASS holds that interim tests are a distinct category, are not proximate to learning as it develops, and therefore do not serve the purpose of informing ongoing teaching and learning; it reported no meaningful evidence that they enhance student learning.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson keeps interim/benchmark as a separate label defined by administration schedule and function, and applies the same purpose test used throughout: an interim test is being used formatively only when its results actually change instruction. It reports the FAST SCASS evidence statement as of 2012 rather than as a permanent finding.

positions: Formative assessment literature commonly treats feedback as the active ingredient.
Kluger and DeNisi found an average positive effect (d = .41) but that over one third of feedback interventions lowered performance, with effectiveness falling as attention shifts toward the self.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches feedback as a variable-direction intervention rather than a reliably positive one, and links the mechanism (attention to the self rather than the task) to the practical rule about grades crowding out comments.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft asserted nothing substantive about assessment. Its In 30 Seconds, Why This Matters, College Version, vocabulary, worked example, mistakes and quick-check items were template text that named the topic without defining it, and none of it was retained.
The draft's vocabulary entry defined the topic as 'a foundational Education concept covered in this lesson', which is circular and was discarded.
The draft's Eli-10 analogy ('a label on a toolbox drawer') carried no information about the formative/summative distinction and was replaced.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire draft with sourced content built around the central point that purpose and use, not the instrument, determine whether an assessment is formative or summative.
Added the historical origin (Scriven 1967 on curricula; Bloom 1969 on student learning) that the draft omitted entirely.
Added the neighbouring labels - diagnostic, interim/benchmark, curriculum-embedded, screening, progress monitoring - which are routinely conflated with formative assessment.
Added the honest evidence section: the 0.4-0.7 range is presented as a 1998 claim that later work has not confirmed, never as a fact.
Added the finding that feedback can lower performance, which contradicts the common classroom assumption that more feedback is always better.
Kept reliability and validity to a single passing sentence and excluded rubric construction, per the unit's topic boundaries.
